title: Burnham v. Superior Court (1990)
summary: Personal service on an individual voluntarily present in the forum supports jurisdiction over an unrelated claim: all nine Justices agreed, but Scalia’s plurality rested on the rule’s unbroken historical pedigree while Brennan’s four Justices required and found contemporary fairness.
notes:
This is an individual’s voluntary presence. It does not decide all cases involving fraudulent inducement, compelled attendance, immunity, or service on a corporation’s agent. Compare Tickle and Wyman before extending the rule to deception.

Dennis Burnham was a New Jersey resident served with his estranged wife's California divorce petition during a three-day visit; the Scalia opinion reasons that jurisdiction based on physical presence alone satisfies due process because it is one of the continuing traditions of our legal system, while Brennan's concurrence reasons that a visitor knowingly avails himself of the state's benefits and protections and can reasonably anticipate being sued there.

sections.Parties: Dennis Burnham, a New Jersey resident, was the husband and defendant in a California divorce proceeding; he petitioned for relief from the California court’s assertion of jurisdiction and then sought Supreme Court review. Francie Burnham, his estranged wife, had moved to California with their children and filed the action there. The Superior Court appears in the caption because Dennis sought extraordinary relief against the trial court’s ruling rather than appealing a final decree.
sections.Material Facts: The Burnhams married in West Virginia in 1976 and moved to New Jersey in 1977, where their two children were born. In July 1987 they agreed to separate: Francie would move to California with the children and file for divorce on grounds of irreconcilable differences. In October Dennis instead filed a New Jersey divorce complaint alleging desertion, without having a summons issued or serving Francie. She filed in California in early January 1988. Later that month Dennis traveled to southern California on business and then to the Bay Area to see his children; he took the older child to San Francisco for the weekend, and on January 24, when he returned the child to Francie’s home, he was personally served with the California summons and petition. His presence was voluntary and knowing, his visits were brief, and nothing about the divorce arose from his California activities.
sections.Procedural History: Dennis made a special appearance and moved to quash service for lack of personal jurisdiction, arguing that a few short trips for business and to see his children were insufficient contacts for the divorce action. The Superior Court denied the motion. He sought mandamus in the California Court of Appeal for the First Appellate District, which denied relief on the ground that personal service on a defendant physically present in the state is a valid basis for jurisdiction. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to review that judgment and affirmed. It decided nothing about marital status, property, support or custody, or about the effect of the unserved New Jersey complaint.
sections.Issue: Does the Fourteenth Amendment permit a state court to exercise personal jurisdiction over a nonresident individual personally served while voluntarily and temporarily in the state, when the lawsuit does not arise from the activities that brought him there? After International Shoe and Shaffer, must the plaintiff separately establish claim-related minimum contacts despite valid in-state personal service?
sections.Holding: Yes, jurisdiction was proper, and no, no further showing was required on these facts. Justice Scalia announced the judgment, joined by Chief Justice Rehnquist and Justice Kennedy and, for most parts, Justice White; Justice Brennan, joined by Justices Marshall, Blackmun and O’Connor, concurred in the judgment; Justices White and Stevens each wrote separately. All nine agreed that personal service on Dennis while he was voluntarily in California supported jurisdiction, but no single rationale for transient (“tag”) jurisdiction commanded five votes. The California Court of Appeal was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: Scalia began with the long acceptance, in English and American courts around the adoption of the Fourteenth Amendment and continuously since, of jurisdiction over individuals served within the state; an established and still-followed method helps define the traditional notions of fair play and substantial justice that International Shoe invoked. International Shoe expanded jurisdiction over absent defendants by supplying a way to judge their relationship to a state when service within it was unavailable; it did not make actual presence insufficient. Shaffer concerned absent individuals whose unrelated property a statute assigned to the forum, and its broad language did not compel identical treatment of someone personally present; this part had only three votes. Brennan read International Shoe and Shaffer to require every jurisdictional rule, old or new, to satisfy contemporary due process; history mattered because it gave fair warning, not because it was conclusive. A voluntary visitor uses the state’s roads and police, participates in its economy and may invoke its courts, so exempting him from suit would create an asymmetry. Because Dennis was knowingly and voluntarily in California, jurisdiction was fair.

learning.why: California could exercise jurisdiction over an individual served while voluntarily visiting the state, although the Justices disagreed about the governing rationale.

topics.cp-tag-jurisdiction: Personal service on an individual voluntarily present in the forum supported jurisdiction.
topics.cp-precedent: The Justices agreed on the result but divided between a historical explanation and a fairness analysis.
topics.cp-service: The individual was physically served during his California visit.
topics.cp-territorial: Scalia grounds transient jurisdiction in the Pennoyer-era territorial tradition.
topics.cp-due-process: The Justices split over whether due process is defined by tradition or by contemporary fairness.
topics.minimum-contacts: Brennan's opinion applies the minimum-contacts framework to in-state service, while Scalia treats it as inapplicable.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice White agreed that personal service sufficed and would not upset a traditional rule absent a showing that it was so arbitrary in its general operation as to violate due process, at least where the defendant’s presence is intentional; he did not join Scalia’s full treatment of Shaffer. Justice Stevens found the historical evidence, continuing consensus, fairness and common sense together sufficient and saw no need to resolve the broader dispute; his was the ninth vote for the judgment, leaving neither rationale an opinion of the Court.
